mechaber.he: דין המחייב עצמו לחבירו. ובו ב סעיפים: המחייב עצמו בממון לאחר בלא תנאי אע"פ שלא היה חייב לו כלום ה"ז חייב כיצד האומר לעדים הוו עלי עדים שאני חייב לפלוני מנה או שכתב לו בשטר הריני חייב לך מנה אע"פ שאין שם עדים או שאמר לו בפני עדים הריני חייב לך מנה בשטר אע"פ שלא אמר אתם עידי הואיל ואמר בשטר ה"ז כמו שאמר הוו עלי עדים וחייב לשלם אע"פ ששניהם מודים והעדים יודעים שלא היה לו אצלו כלום שהרי חייב עצמו כמו שישתעבד הערב וכ"ש כשכותב לאחד קבלתי ממך כך וכך על החוב שיש בידך דהוי מחילה אע"ג דידעינן דלא קבל (ב"י סי' ע"ג בשם הריטב"א):
mechaber.en: The Law of One Who Voluntarily Obligates Himself to Another. Two seifim. A person who unconditionally obligates himself to pay money to another is liable even though he previously owed him nothing. For example, if he says to witnesses, 'Be witnesses for me that I owe so-and-so one hundred zuz,' writes in a document, 'I owe you one hundred zuz,' even without witnesses, or says before witnesses, 'I owe you one hundred zuz by document,' then even if he did not say, 'You are my witnesses,' his reference to a document is equivalent to appointing them as witnesses. He must pay even if both parties admit, and the witnesses know, that he never owed anything, because he obligated himself just as a guarantor binds himself. {Rama: All the more so, if a person writes, 'I received such-and-such from you toward the debt you hold against me,' it constitutes a waiver even when we know that he received nothing (Beit Yosef, siman 73, in the name of the Ritva).}

baer_hetev.he:
כלום. היינו שיודע שאינו חייב לו ומחייב עצמו כמו מתנה אבל אם מחייב עצמו מחמת שסבור שהוא חייב לו ואח"כ נודע שטעה אפילו מסר לו שטר בעדים אינו כלום והוא פשוט לקמן סי' קכ"ו סי"ג וכמה דוכתי דכל קנין בטעות חוזר. ש"ך:
האומר. כתב הסמ"ע דרבים חולקים בזה וס"ל דלא מהני מה שאומר בע"פ כ"א בהודא' שכבר חייב לו אבל אם בא להתחייב לו עתה בדיבור לא מהני כ"א כשכתב לו בשטר כן או באמר אני חייב לך מנה בשטר ומן התימא על המחבר והרמ"א שכתבו סתם בלי חולק עכ"ל וע"ל סי' ל"ט מ"ש שם בס"ק ג':
שכתב. כתב הב"ח דוקא כתב בכתב ידו אבל אם לא כתב בכת"י ולא חתם תחתיו כלל משמע בטור לר"ת אע"פ שמסרו לו בפני עדים אפי' מבני חורין לא גבי דמצי למימר משטה אני בך והש"ך השיג ע"ז וכתב דכיון דעידי מסיר' כרתי מה בכך שאינו כתב ידו כיון שמסרו לו בפני עדים הם מפקי לקלא וגובה אפילו ממשעבדי ולא שייך משטה אני בך בכה"ג כו' ע"ש באריכות:
הערב. פירוש כשקודם שחתמו העדים כתב בשטר פ' לוה מפ' ופלוני ערב ואח"כ חתמו העדים דמשתעבד הערב אפילו לא קנו מידו ואף לאחר שהלוהו כיון דכתב ליה בשטר כמ"ש בסי' קכ"ט עכ"ל הסמ"ע וכתב עליו הש"ך דלא דק דהא ס"ל להרמב"ם והטור והמחבר לקמן סי' קכ"ט ס"ד דצריך קנין בערב היוצא קודם חיתום שטרות אלא כוונתם כאן לומר כמו שישתעבד הערב אע"פ שאינו חייב גם הלו' יכול להשתעבד כן עכ"ד (* א"ה לדעתי החלוש' אין זו השג' כ"כ דאף שבדברי הרמב"ם אין לפרש כך דהוא סובר דצריך קנין אפילו קודם חיתום שטרות מ"מ להט"ו יש לפרש כן דהא הטור כתב בפשיטות בסי' קכ"ט דקודם חיתום שטרות אם כתב ופלוני ערב א"צ קנין וגם המחבר כתב שם בס"ד דיש פלוגת' אפילו בלאחר חיתום שטרות י"א דא"צ קנין ואחר כך כתב ולהרמב"ם אפילו קודם חיתום צריך קנין וע"ש בס"ז בסמ"ע וט"ז וק"ל):
כשכותב. ע"ל סי' פ"א סכ"ט דה"ה אם הודה בע"פ שקבל החוב שבשטר או שמחל לו הוי מחילה עכ"ל הסמ"ע (ובש"ך שם ס"ק ע"ב כתב דבמוחל ותפיס שטרא הוי ספיקא דדינא ע"ש):
baer_hetev.en:
Nothing. This means that the person knows he does not presently owe the money and voluntarily obligates himself, comparable to making a gift. But if he obligates himself because he mistakenly believes that he owes the money and later discovers the mistake, even if he delivered a written instrument before witnesses it is ineffective. This is obvious from siman 126, seif 13, and many other places, because every kinyan made in error is reversible. Shach.
One who says. The Sema writes that many authorities disagree and hold that an oral statement is effective only as an admission that he already owes the money. If he seeks to create a new obligation merely by speaking, it is ineffective unless he writes it in a document or says, "I owe you one maneh in a document." It is surprising that the Mechaber and Rama state the rule without mentioning dissent. See above, siman 39, seif katan 3.
That he wrote. The Bach writes that this requires the obligor's own handwriting. If he neither wrote it in his own hand nor signed beneath it, the Tur implies according to Rabbeinu Tam that even if he delivered the document before witnesses he cannot collect even from unencumbered property, because the obligor may say, "I was joking with you." The Shach disagrees. Since witnesses to delivery give the document legal force, it makes no difference that it is not in the obligor's handwriting. Delivery before witnesses creates publicity, and the obligee may collect even from encumbered property. In such circumstances a claim of joking is inapplicable. See the Shach at length.
The guarantor. The Sema explains: where, before the witnesses sign, the document states, "So-and-so borrowed from so-and-so, and so-and-so is guarantor," and the witnesses then sign, the guarantor becomes bound even without a kinyan. This applies even if the guarantee was added after the loan, because it was written in the document, as explained in siman 129. The Shach responds that this is imprecise, because Rambam, the Tur, and the Mechaber in siman 129, seif 4, require a kinyan for a guarantor whose obligation appears before the witnesses' signatures. Their intent here is only that just as a guarantor can create an obligation even though he did not previously owe the debt, so too a borrower can create a new obligation upon himself. In my humble opinion this criticism is not decisive. Although Rambam cannot be explained as the Sema suggests because he requires a kinyan even before the signatures, the Tur and Mechaber can be read that way. The Tur plainly writes in siman 129 that if "and so-and-so is guarantor" is written before the witnesses' signatures no kinyan is required. The Mechaber there records a dispute even regarding a guarantee written after the signatures, with some saying no kinyan is needed, and then adds that according to Rambam even one written before the signatures requires a kinyan. See there, seif 7, and the Sema and Taz.
When he writes. See below, siman 81, seif 29. The same applies if a creditor orally admits that he received payment of the debt stated in a document, or orally waives it; the waiver is effective. Thus the Sema. The Shach there, seif katan 72, writes that where a creditor waives the debt but still retains the document, the law remains doubtful.

beer_hagolah.he:
א) הרמב"ם בפי"ח מהלכות מכירה וכתב הכ"מ שהוא נלמד מהא דאמרינן ולודי איסור דהני זוזי וכו' וליקנינהו באודיתא ב"ב דף קמ"ט ע"א
ב) כ' ה"ה שפסק כר' יוחנן וכאוקימתא דגמרא שם כגון שאמר בפני עדים חייב אני לך מנה בשטר כתובות דף ק"י ע"ב וכפי פירושו שבא להתחייב בלא הלואה וכיון שהזכיר מלת שטר ה"ז כמי שבא להתחייב ואמר אתם עידי ומכל שכן אם כתב לו בשטר הריני חייב לך מנה ומסרו לו בעדים במ"ד דעידי מסירה קונים א"נ שהיה השטר בכתב ידי המתחייב ונתנו בינו לבינו ולגבות מנכסים בני חורין וכו' וכתב שדעת ההלכות נראה כדע' המחבר
beer_hagolah.en:
The Rambam, chapter 18 of Hilkhot Mekhirah. The Kesef Mishneh writes that this is learned from the statement, 'Let Issur admit that these monies belong to him,' etc., and acquire them by admission, Bava Batra 149a.
The Maggid Mishneh writes that he rules like Rabbi Yochanan and according to the Gemara's interpretation there, such as where he said before witnesses, 'I owe you one hundred by document,' Ketubot 110b. According to the Rambam's explanation, he seeks to obligate himself without a loan, and since he mentioned the word 'document' it is as though he came to obligate himself and said, 'You are my witnesses.' All the more so if he wrote in a document, 'I owe you one hundred,' and delivered it before witnesses, according to the view that witnesses of delivery effect acquisition. Alternatively, the document was in the obligor's own handwriting and he gave it privately, in which case collection is from unencumbered property. The Maggid Mishneh writes that the Rif's view appears to agree with the Mechaber.

beur_hagra.he:
(ליקוט) המחייב כו'. כפי' הרי"ף ור"ת כמו שהוכיח הרי"ף שם מדפריך מהנושא ומפדיון הבן אע"ג שאינו פדוי ומערב אלמא בכה"ג איירי וז"ש כמו שישתעבד הערב (ע"כ):
(ליקוט) המחייב כו'. כפי' הרי"ף דלא כרש"י שמפ' בשטר הודאה והוכיח הרי"ף ממש"ש תנן הנושא כו' כ' לכהן כו' כתנאי ערב כו' ובכ"ז אין חייב כלום ועבה"ג וכפי' תוס' שם וז"ש הרמב"ם וש"ע כמו שישתעבד הערב (ע"כ):
(ליקוט) כיצד כו'. שם אי דאמר כו' (ע"כ):
(ליקוט) כיצד האומר כו' כפי' הרי"ף דא"ל חייב כו' שא"ל כן בע"פ וכ"ש באומר הוו עלי כו' דאף ר"ל מודה כמש"ש ומ"ש או שכתב כו' שם ת"ש כתב לכהן כו'. אבל הרמב"ן ורשב"א פי' כפי' ר"ת דוקא בכתב לו בשטר אבל באומר חייב כו' או אתם עדי לאו כלום דאין מתחיי' בדברים וכמ"ש בב"ב קע"ג ב' בההוא הנאה כו' משא"כ כאן ולכן לאחר מתן מעות לא קנה בדברים אלא בקנין וכן כאן דוקא בקנין או בשטר וכן בב"מ צ"ד א' אפ"ת כו' בההוא כו' ומ"ש בכתובו' שם ה"ד אי כו' ס"ד. כפירש"י בהודאה וזה דקא' מ"ט דר"ל דלפי' הרי"ף האיך פשיט' להו כ"כ אבל הרמב"ם נזהר מזה דאין ראיה מערב דלה"ק שם בההיא משום דאסמכת' היא כמ"ש בגמ' שם וכן בש"ש בב"מ שם ג"כ אסמכת' היא כמש"ש ס"ו ב' כל דאי כו' וז"ש בלא תנאי וכ' ברמב"ם שם ואינה אסמכת' כו' (ע"כ):
או שכ'. או שאמר. כ"ז ל' הרמב"ם וכל' א' כ' ר"ת וכל' ב' כ' רי"ף:
(ליקוט) אע"פ ששניהם כו' מהא דאודית' קמ"ט א' וכפי' תוס' שם ד"ה ש"מ ונראה לר"י כו' וכמ"ש תוס' שם מ"ד ב' בד"ה דלא כו' ונראה לר"ת כו' (ע"כ):
שהרי חייב. ערי"ף שם:
וכ"ש. נדרים ס"ג ב':
(ליקוט) וכ"ש כשכותב כו'. דבזה אף רש"י מודה (ע"כ):
beur_hagra.en:
(Collected note) One who obligates, etc. According to the Rif and Rabbeinu Tam, as the Rif proves there from the challenge from HaNoseh and from redemption of the firstborn, even though the son is not redeemed, and from a guarantor. Thus the case concerns one who creates an obligation in this way. This is the meaning of "just as a guarantor becomes obligated." (End of collected note.)
(Collected note) One who obligates, etc. According to the Rif, unlike Rashi, who explains it as a document of admission. The Rif proves it from the Gemara's statement, "we learned, one who marries, etc.; he wrote to the Kohen, etc.; like the condition of a guarantor, etc." In all these cases there was no prior liability. See Beer HaGolah and Tosafot's explanation there. Therefore the Rambam and Shulchan Aruch write "just as a guarantor becomes obligated." (End of collected note.)
(Collected note) How so, etc. There: "if he said, etc." (End of collected note.)
(Collected note) How so, one who says, etc. According to the Rif's explanation, he says orally, "I am obligated, etc." All the more so if he says, "be my witnesses, etc.," for even Reish Lakish concedes in such a case, as stated there. "Or he wrote, etc." is from the challenge, "come and hear, he wrote to the Kohen, etc." Ramban and Rashba, however, explain like Rabbeinu Tam that it is effective only if written in a document. Merely saying "I am obligated, etc." or "you are my witnesses" is nothing, because one does not create a new obligation through words alone, as stated in Bava Batra 173b regarding "by virtue of that benefit, etc." Unlike there, after the money was already given a guarantor does not become obligated through words alone but only through a kinyan; so too here, only through a kinyan or document. Likewise Bava Metzia 94a: "even if you say, etc., by virtue of that, etc." As for Ketubot there, "what are the circumstances? If, etc.," according to Rashi's approach it initially thought it was an admission. This explains why the Gemara asks, "what is Reish Lakish's reason?" According to the Rif, why would the law have seemed so obvious? The Rambam, however, was careful here: the analogy to a guarantor is imperfect because there the Gemara initially asks that it is an asmachta, and likewise a paid bailee's undertaking in Bava Metzia there is an asmachta, as stated on 66b, "every 'if,' etc." Therefore the Rambam specifies "without a condition" and writes that it is not an asmachta. (End of collected note.)
Or he wrote. Or he said. All this is the Rambam's wording. The first phrase follows Rabbeinu Tam and the second the Rif.
(Collected note) Although both, etc. From the case of the admission in Bava Batra 149a, according to Tosafot there, s.v. "Shema Mina," "Ri explains, etc.," and Tosafot there 44b, s.v. "Delo, etc.," "Rabbeinu Tam explains, etc." (End of collected note.)
For he has obligated. See Rif there.
And certainly. Nedarim 63b.
(Collected note) And certainly when he writes, etc. In that case even Rashi agrees. (End of collected note.)

chelkat_mechokek.he: שנתאכלו המעות. לא דמי לאומר לחבירו משוך פרה זו ולא תקנה אלא לאחר ל' דלא קנה (כמבואר בח"ה סי' קצ"ז סעי' ז') דשאני משיכה דלאחר ל' אין במשיכה ממש ובמה יקנה אבל הכא אם היא תחזור צריכה להחזיר המעות הוי כאלו נתן לה מעות בסוף ל' ומיהו אם הוא חוזר אינה חייבת להחזיר לו וכ"כ הר"ן:
chelkat_mechokek.en: Eat the farms. It is not enough to say to his father to pull this cow, and not to buy it, but after Hashem’s grace, he will not be given, but if he comes back, he will give her an end to Hashem, and who if he does not return to him

kessef_hakodashim.he: סעיף א' (שכתב לו בשטר) מ"ש בחו"מ בסי' מ' התחייבות ע"י שכותב בשטר התחייבות אין החיוב חל רק על ידי מסירה ליד מי שנתחייב לו וכן הוא לשון הש"כ ז"ל והאורו"ת ז"ל שם: וגם אם מסר השטר ליד נכרי אין חיוב חל עי"ז. וגם אם מסר ליד יודי אין חיוב חל רק אם אמר לו שמוסר ומזכה על ידו שיחול החיוב: לשון שבין גוים מורה על חיוב ובלשון עם בני ישראל אינו מורה חיוב כגון לשון התקשרות ששמעתי שבלשון גוים הוא חיוב. גם שהכתב ולשון של גוים מ"מ כיון שיודי חתם את עצמי על השטר יש לומר שאינו מורה חיוב: כתבתי במק"א שתקיעת כף הנהוג בתורת סיטומתא יש לומר שאין בו כח להטיל חיוב כי קנין סודר שסתמו לכתיבה עומד הרי זה כחייב אני בשטר שלשון זה יכול לגרום חיוב חדש באודיתא מה שאין כן סיטומתא שאין סתמיותה עומד לקנין שטר בכתיבה אולי אין בה כח להטיל חיוב וכשנהגו להתחייב בזה מ"מ אין בו כח באולי ובמקום שלא נהגו כלל בזה רק לקנין ולא נודע מנהג להתחייב בזה כנראה דפשיטא דלא שייך בזה צד סיטומתא לחיוב וצלע"ע:
kessef_hakodashim.en: Seif 1. That he wrote to him in a document. Siman 40 teaches that where a person creates a new obligation by writing it in a document, the obligation does not take effect merely through writing. The document must be delivered to the person in whose favor the obligation is created. This is also the language of the Shach and Urim VeTumim. Delivery to a non-Jew does not itself make the obligation effective. Even delivery to a Jew is insufficient unless the obligor states that he is delivering it to that person in order to transfer and acquire it on behalf of the beneficiary so that the obligation will take effect. Some expressions used in non-Jewish commercial language signify a binding obligation even though the corresponding wording among Jews does not. I have heard, for example, that a particular term meaning "engagement" or "commitment" functions as an obligation in their legal usage. Still, even if the instrument is written in their language and script, where a Jew signs it one must determine whether Jewish legal usage regards that expression as creating a personal obligation. I have written elsewhere that the customary handshake or handclasp treated as situmta may not necessarily have the power to create a new personal debt. A kinyan sudar is ordinarily connected with preparation of a written instrument, and can therefore function like the formal statement "I owe you" in a document, which creates a new obligation through admission. Situmta, by contrast, is a commercial act whose ordinary function is to acquire property, not to create a written personal debt. Unless the local custom specifically uses it to assume obligations, it may lack that power. Where the custom is only to use the act for acquisition and no practice of creating personal liabilities through it is known, it appears clear that situmta does not create such a debt. The matter nevertheless requires further study.

ketzot_hachoshen.he:
[" הוו עלי עדים. בר\"פ הנושא אתמר האומר לחבירו חייב אני לך מנה ר\"י אמר חייב ור\"ל אמר פטור ה\"ד אי דא\"ל אתם עדי מ\"ט דר\"ל דפטור אי דלא א\"ל אתם עדי מ\"ט דר\"י דחייב לעולם דלא קאמר אתם עדי והבמ\"ע דא\"ל חייב אני לך מנה בשטר ר\"י אמר חייב אלימא מלתא דשטרא כמאן דא\"ל אתם עדי דמי ור\"ל אמר פטור לא אלימא מלתא דשטרא ונשנו ונאמרו בזה שלשה שיטות פירש\"י שמחייב עתה בשטר שמסרו לו בפני עדים ולא חתם בו רק שכתב בכת\"י אני חייב לך מנה בשטר ומיירי בהודאה כו' ור\"ת פי' כולה סוגיא בלא הודאה והא דקאמר חייב אני לך מנה בשטר היינו בשטר גמור ורצה להשתעבד ולהתחייב לו מנה בשטר זה בהא פליגי ר\"י סובר אלימא מלתא דשטרא לאקנוי בי' בשטר זה כמי שהודה בפני עדים ועיין שם בתוספות שכתבו צ\"ל ואין הדמיון טוב אלא איידי דנקט לעיל דא\"ל אתם עדי נקט נמי הכא כמאן דא\"ל אתם עדי ואין לתמו' היאך משתעבד בשטר זה הא אין מטלטלי ketzot_hachoshen.en:
Be witnesses for me. At the beginning of Perek HaNosei the Gemara records a dispute concerning one who says to another, "I owe you a maneh." Rabbi Yochanan obligates and Reish Lakish exempts. The Gemara ultimately establishes the case as one who says, "I owe you a maneh in a document." Rashi explains this as an existing admission written and delivered before witnesses. Rabbeinu Tam explains it as a new undertaking created through a full written instrument. Rif and Rambam interpret it differently: he says orally, "I owe you a maneh in a document," and the very formulation creates liability even though both parties and the witnesses know that no prior debt existed. The later authorities ask how mere words can create such an obligation without kinyan, document, or consideration. The correct explanation is that Rambam relies on acquisition through formal admission. A person's legal admission can itself transfer property or create rights even where both sides know that the factual content of the admission was previously false. Tosafot explicitly recognizes acquisition by admission in the case of Issur the convert, and such admission operates for a healthy person as well as one dying. Thus Rambam does not hold that arbitrary words alone create obligations. The operative mechanism is a formal admission, which is itself a valid mode of acquisition. This also explains why the Gemara compares the phrase "in a document" to saying, "You are my witnesses." A formal admission requires the legal setting that gives the statement testimonial force. One must know, however, that this mode of acquisition by admission is not completed in private. Ordinary modes of acquisition do not require witnesses except to prevent later denial, because the acquisition itself occurs independently. Admission is different. Its very legal force depends upon a formal witnessed admission. If he says it privately, or even before witnesses without establishing them as witnesses where the circumstances require that, there is no acquisition by admission. This resolves Tosafot's question in Bava Metzia concerning one standing at his granary who transfers produce and then redeems second tithe on money in his house. Tosafot asks why he does not transfer the money through admission, as Issur did. Since the Gemara's case can be one without witnesses, there is no difficulty. An ordinary sudar kinyan could still work privately because witnesses are needed only to prove it. Admission acquisition cannot. This distinction also answers later writers who assumed that admission is merely another private mode of acquisition. It is not. Its formal testimonial character is part of the acquisition itself.

One who says to witnesses, "Be witnesses for me," etc. In Derishah I explained the source Rambam relied upon for this law and that many authorities disagree. They hold that an oral statement of this kind can help only as an admission of an already-existing debt. To create a new obligation now through speech alone is ineffective unless he writes such an undertaking in a document or says, "I owe you one maneh by document," which Rambam himself accepts. The Tur, although quoting Rambam's language, omitted this opening rule because he did not accept it. It is therefore surprising that the Mechaber and Rama state it without recording any dissent. See what I wrote at the beginning of siman 39 in the name of Hagahot Ashri.

לבו לחלוק מסברא על התו' והתו' שהביא בעצמו שכתבו דמהני כשמוד' בהודאה גמורה אפי' בלא עדים וכ"כ התומים בכמה דוכתי בפשיטות וכן נראה' דבכ"מ דאתם עידי מהני הודא' גמורה ג"כ מהני דבמקום דחשיב הודא' נגד טענת השטאה חשוב ג"כ קנין:
netivot_hamishpat_beurim.en: You are my witnesses. Many authorities disagree with Mechaber's two rules concerning the formula 'You are my witnesses' and a written statement, 'I owe you one hundred,' holding that a person cannot create a gratuitous obligation except through a complete deed or his own handwriting. This dispute concerns a case where he expressly reveals that he is not admitting a preexisting debt but is creating a new obligation now. If he simply says, 'You are my witnesses that I owe so-and-so one hundred,' the statement is ordinarily treated as an admission. If the claimant says the debt really preexisted, the speaker cannot later retract by claiming he merely intended to create a new gratuitous obligation and has changed his mind. Even if it is independently known that no prior debt existed, an unqualified formulation of admission can itself function as an *odita*, a recognized conveyancing admission, and all authorities agree that an *odita* can transfer rights. Shach's statement that if he admits no prior debt he is exempt refers to a case where he also says his admission was mistaken. Otherwise the unqualified admission stands. I also reject the suggestion that according to Rosh a handwritten obligation requires delivery witnesses in every case. In money, the party's own admission can supply the necessary force against himself even without delivery witnesses; only where the document is intended to prejudice third parties, such as purchasers, can lack of delivery witnesses prevent the document from operating against them. Ketzot HaChoshen's claim that an *odita* itself requires witnesses is therefore incorrect. Wherever a complete admission is effective against a plea of joking, it can likewise have conveyancing force.

rabbi_akiva_eiger.he: [שו"ע] הוו עלי עדים שאני. נ"ב דעת הש"ך לקמן סי' פ"א ס"ק מ"ט דאף בהודה דרך הודאה גמורה דלא שייך השטאה וגם הי' ההודאה בפניו דל"ש השבע' מ"מ א"י לחייב עצמו בכך אא"כ אמר א"ע ומכ"ש היכי דיכול לומר משטה אם מודה שכוון בהודאה להתחייב עצמו באמת דלא מהני וכ"כ להדיא בסמ"ע ס"ק ב' ואו"ת שם חלק עליהם דאין א"ע מעלה בזה לענין החיוב אלא העיקר כל שכוון להודאה גמורה בלא השטאה יכול לחייב עצמו עיי"ש:
rabbi_akiva_eiger.en: [Shulchan Aruch] Be witnesses for me that I owe. Note: The Shach below, siman 81, subparagraph 49, holds that even where a person made a full admission in a manner where joking is not applicable, and the admission was made in the claimant’s presence so that the defense of attempting to induce a false admission does not apply, he still cannot obligate himself unless he says, "You are my witnesses." Certainly, where he could claim that he was joking, even if he admits that he truly intended by his admission to obligate himself, it is ineffective. The Sema, subparagraph 2, writes this explicitly. Urim VeTumim there disagrees and holds that saying "You are my witnesses" adds nothing to the creation of liability. The essential point is that whenever he intended a genuine admission without joking, he can obligate himself. See there.

siftei_kohen.he:
[" המחייב עצמו כו' היינו שיודע שאינו חייב לו ומחייב עצמו כמו מתנה אבל מי שמודה לחברו בחזקת שחייב לו ואח\"כ נודע שטעה ונתברר הדבר בעדים או שהודה לו מלוה שאינו חייב לו הרי זה הודאה בטעות ואינה כלום אפי' מסר לו שטר בעדים ועדים חתומים בו כמ\"ש הטור והוא פשוט לקמן סי' קכ\"ו סי ג וכמה דוכתי דכל קנין בטעות חוזר:"]
[" כיצד האומר לעדים כו'. כ' בסמ\"ע שרבים חולקים בזה וס\"ל דלא מהני כשבא להתחייב עתה כ\"א כשכתב לו כן בשטר או באומר אני חייב לך מנה בשטר כו' ולא דק דה\"ל לכתוב דחולקין וס\"ל דאף באומר אני חייב לך מנה בשטר לא מהני רק כשכתב לו כן בשטר כמ\"ש ה\"ה פי\"א מה' מכירה בשם הרמב\"ן והרשב\"א ושאר מפרשים להדיא ע\"ש וכ' עוד ה' המגיד שם וז\"ל ולפי שטה זו אין שום צד שיהיה. חייב אלא כשכתב לו שטר ונמצא שהם חולקין על המחבר אשני חלוקין משלשה שכ' עכ\"ל וכן משמע בר\"ן ריש פ' הנושא לפי שטה זו שכ' דבדברים בעלמא אי אפשר שיתחייב אלא בקבלת כסף או בקנין או בשטר כו' ע\"ש ולרש\"י בכל גווני לא מהני כשמתחייב עכשיו וכמ\"ש ב\"י לדעת רש\"י וכ\"פ בשלטי גבורים ר\"פ הנושא בשם ריא\"ז ז\"ל וז\"ל הבא להתחייב בדבר שאינו מחויב בו במקום שאינו חובת ממון כגון שאמר הריני מחויב ליתן לך מנה אע\"פ שאמר לעדים אתם עדי ואע\"פ שכ' לו שטר חתום ומסרו לו ה\"ז אינו מתחייב אא\"כ קנו מידו כב\"ה עכ\"ל ועיין בריטב\"א ר\"פ הנושא וע\"ל ס\"ק ה':"]
[" האומר לעדים הוו עלי עדים שאני חייב לפלוני מנה כו'. בזה וכן בחילוק הג' שא\"ל בפני עדים הריני חייב לך מנה בשטר אינו גובה אלא מבני חורין אבל בחילוק האמצעי כשכתב לו בשטר אני חייב לך מנה ומסר השטר בפני עדים גובה ממשעבדי למאן דאמר עידי מסירה כרתי אפי' אינו כת' ידו וכשלא מסר לו בפני עדים גובה מבני חורין אם הוא כת' ידו וכמ\"ש לקמן ס\"ק ה' ובחילוק האמצעי מודים הרמב\"ן והרשב\"א וכן דעת הר\"ן וה\"ה וכן דעת התוס' בשם ר\"ת והרא\"ש וטור ושאר פוסקים וכן כ' הריטב\"א ר\"פ הנושא ששטת ר\"ת נכונה היא וכן עיקר ודלא כשלטי הגבורים שהבאתי בסמוך ס\"ק ב' וה\"ה כשכתבו עדים שטר וכתבו בו שהתחייב עצמו וצוה לכתוב שטר מהני אף להרמב\"ן ורשב\"א ופוסקים הנ\"ל וכן מוכח בהר\"ן ר\"פ הנושא ע\"ש גם מ\"ש ולר\"ל אפי' בשטר שחתמו בו עדים לא מהני כו' ע\"ש ודו\"ק:"]
[" הוו עלי עדים כו'. ה\"ה כ' שהרמב\"ן והרשב\"א ושאר מפרשים חולקי' והביאו ראיות שאין אדם מתחייב בדברים אפי' באתם עדי בלא קנין ובלא שטר כו' ואולי הם ראיות שהביא הר\"ן ר\"פ הנושא וז\"ל דהא בערב נמי בעינן או קנין או מתן מעות ובההיא הנאה דקא מהימן ליה ובפ' הזהב (בבא מציעא דף נ\"ח ע\"א) נמי אמרינן גבי שומר קרקעות בשקנו מידן וכן בפ' השואל גבי מתנה שומר חנם להיות כשואל אקשינן במאי בדברים ואצטריך לפרוקי בההיא הנאה דקא מהימן ליה כו' וכ' שם הר\"ן בסוף דבריו דלדעת הרי\"ף והרמב\"ם י\"ל דכי איצטריך לאוקמא בשקנו מידו לאו דוקא דהוא הדין באומר אתם עדי מהני דהא על כרחך ה\"ה דמצי לאוקמא בשחייב עצמו בשטר כיון דקיימא לן כר' יוחנן אלא דנקט קנו מידו לפי שהיא ההקנאה היותר רגילה ובערב היינו טעמא דלא מהני ביה אתם עדי לפי שהוא דומה לאסמכתא זה [ולי] נראה לדעת הרי\"ף והרמב\"ם דדוקא הכא מהני כשחייב עצמו בשטר או באתם עדי כיון שמתחייב עצמו מיד בלי תנא' מה שא\"כ בשומר קרקעות ושואל כיון שאינו מתחייב מיד רק אם יאבד דמי לערב שכ' הר\"ן גופיה דדמי לאסמכתא ולא מהני רק בקנין וכן מדוקדק למעיין בלשון הרמב\"ם שהתחיל המחייב עצמו בממון לאחר בלא תנאי כלל כו' חייב שדבר זה מתנה היא ואינה אסמכתא כיצד האומר לעדים כו' (והביאו ר' ירוחם נתיב ט\"ו ח\"ג ע\"ש) דלאיזה צורך כ' בלא תנאי כלל כו' ואינו אסמכתא כו' אלא כוונתו כמ\"ש כנ\"ל ברור:"]
[" או שכ' לו בשטר כו'. כ' הבית חדש דוקא כתב בכתב ידו אבל אם לא כת' בכתב ידו ולא חתם תחתיו כלל משמע בטור לר\"ת אע\"פ שמסרו לו בפני העדים אפילו מבני חורין לא גבי דמצי למימר משטה אני בך והכי משמע במרדכי להדיא ואיתא נמי בהגה אשר\"י עכ\"ל ותמיה לי' דכיון דעדי מסירה כרתי מה בכך שאינו כתב ידו וכיון שמסרו לו בפני עדים ועדי מסירה מפקי לקלא גובה אפי' ממשעבדי אע\"פ שאינו כת' ידו ולא שייך משטה אני בך בכה\"ג ואפי' לגירסת הסמ\"ע בהמחבר לקמן סעיף ב' והוא שיהיה כתב ידו שאינו יכול להזדייף כו' היינו משום דיכול לזייף וכמ\"ש בסמ\"ע שם ס\"ק ו' הא לאו הכי גובה אפי' ממשעבדי אע\"פ שאינו כת\"י הלוה וכ\"כ הטור ס\"ס ס\"ט בהדיא בפשיטות דאפי' אינו כתב ידו עדי מסירה כרתי וא\"כ ה\"ה הכא דלא מסתבר לחלק כלל בין חייב לו כבר בין מתחייב עתה לענין זה וכן משמע להדיא בב\"י שכ' בס\"ס זה וז\"ל ונראה שגם הרמב\"ם יודה בדין זהשכ' הטור בשם ר\"ת שאם כ' בכתב ידו אני פלוני חייב לך מנה ומסר לו השטר בפני עדים חשיב מלוה בשטר דמשום דהוי כתב ידו לא גרע ואע\"ג דלא הוי כלשון שטר כיון שכתוב בו ההודאה ומוסרו בפני עדים סגי עכ\"ל משמע להדיא דבכל ענין הוי מלוה בשטר משום עדי מסירה (ואפשר משמע ליה להב\"ח כן מדהקשו המרדכי והגה' אשר\"י שם אפי' רש\"י שלא חתם תחתיו לימא משטה אני בך ומאי מקשי' הא התם מסר לו בפני עדים אלא ודאי סבירא להו דאף בהודאה יכול לומר משטה אני בך אף שמסר לו בפני עדים וא\"כ כ\"ש במתחייב עצמו אין זה מוכרח די\"ל דס\"ל דמסתמא הסוגי' לפירוש רש\"י מיירי אף למ\"ד אין עידי מסירה כרתי דאי למ\"ד עדי מסירה כרתי מ\"ט דר\"ל דפטר אבל לפי' ר\"ת ניחא דכיון דעכשיו הוא דמתחייב פטר ר\"ל ועוד דכבר סתרתי לקמן סי' פ\"א סעיף י\"ט ס\"ק מ\"ט דברי המרדכי והגהת אשר\"י מכח דברי רש\"י ותוס' ושאר פוסקים ע\"ש): ומ\"ש הב\"ח והכי משמע במרדכי להדיא ואיתא נמי בהגהת אשר\"י ליתא דהמעיין במרדכי והגה' אשר\"י שם יראה להדיא דלא הזכירו כלל שם שיש עדי מסירה אלא כתבו בשם ר\"ת שמתחייב עצמו בכתיבת השטר שכותב לו בכתב ידו אני פלוני חייב לך מנה וחתם תחתיו והיינו לענין לגבות מבני חורין וכמ\"ש בטור לר\"ת. וכן נראה נמי לפרש דברי ר\"ת שבתוס' והרא\"ש ר\"פ הנושא ובזה מיושב לפע\"ד מה שכתבו התוס' שם (דף ק\"ב סוף ע\"א) וז\"ל קשה לפי' ר\"ת הואיל ומוקי להאי כתיבת ערבות שהוא שטר גמור להתחייב בו כשמסר לו בפני עדים מההיא טעמא שמתחייב שום דבר יתחייב לו שעבוד נכסים נמי ע\"י מסירה כמו אם לוה ממנו דעדי מסירה מפקי לקל' עכ\"ל ולפמ\"ש לק\"מ דהך דערבות לא מיירי שמסר לו בפני עדים אלא שכ' לו בכת\"י ואני ערב ושוב מצאתי בחכמת שלמה ובחדושי מהר\"ש אידלש שהרגישו בזה: וכן מ\"ש הטור וז\"ל ור\"ת פי' דלא מיירי בהודאה שמודה בדבר שחייב בו אלא מתחייב לו עתה מנה וכותב בכתב ידו אני פלוני חייב לך ומוסר לו השטר ובמסירת זה השטר מתחייב לו עתה במנה אם מוסרו לו בפני עדים גובה ממשעבדי ואם מוסרו לו בינו לבין עצמו גובה מבני חרי עכ\"ל לא כמו שהבין הב\"ח דלענין עדי מסירה בעינן כתב ידו אלא משום דלעיל מיניה כ' הטור פירש\"י דמיירי שאינו כתב ידו דאי הוה כתב ידו בלאו הכי היה חייב בהודאתו אפי' לא מסר לו השטר בעדים ולא הוו פליגי ר\"ל ור' יוחנן דהא מתני' היא הוציא עליו כתב ידו גובה מבני חורין כתב שר\"ת פי' דלא צריך לדחוקי בהכי אלא אפי' מיירי שהוא כתב ידו מ\"מ פליגי שפיר כיון שאינו מודה שחייב לו כבר ומתחייב לו השתא בכתב זה פליגי אפילו לענין משעבדי כשמוסרו לו בפני עדים או לענין בני חרי כשמוסרו לו בינו לבינו וגם משום דכ' הטור ואם מוסרו לו בינו לבין עצמו גובה מבני חרי הוצרך לכתוב שהוא כתב ידו אבל אה\"נ דאם מוסרו לו בפני עדים לא בעינן שיהא כ' ידו אלא בכל ענין שנכת' שלא יוכל להזדייף גובה ממשעבדי למאן דאמר עדי מסירה כרתי: וראי' ברורה לדברי ממ\"ש ה' המגיד פי\"א מה' מכירה וז\"ל וממילא ראם כתב לו בשטר הריני חייב לך מנה אע\"פ שאין שם עדים בשטר הרי זה קנה וזה שכ' המחבר או שכ' לו שטר כו' ומ\"מ אין זה אלא במסרו לו בעדים וכמ\"ד עידי מסירה קונים אי נמי כגון שהיה השטר בכתב ידי המתחייב ונתנו בינו לבינו לגבות מנכסים בני חורין אבל אם היה כתב ידי אחר ונתנו בינו לבינו ודאי לאו כלום הוא עכ\"ל ומביאו ב\"י וד\"מ ואע\"ג דכ' שם כן להרמב\"ם וכ' שם שהרמב\"ן והרשב\"א חולקין על הרמב\"ם פשיטא דאין חולקין אלא בשני חלוקים דס\"ל להרמב\"ם דאף בלא שטר כגון באתם עידי או שאמר הריני חייב לך בשטר אבל בחילוק הזה שכתב לו שטר כתב ה' המגיד שם להדיא דמודה ליה וא\"כ גם ר\"ת ס\"ל הכי. ומזה שכתבתי נלמד דאם כתב לו בכתב ידו ומסרו בינו לבינו גובה מבני חרי אף להרמב\"ן והרשב\"א וכדמוכח מדברי ה' המגיד להדיא וכן מוכח בטור שכת' כן לשטת ר\"ת והרי ר\"ת ס\"ל להדי' בתו' פרק הנושא כהרמב\"ן והרשב\"א דאינו יכול להתחייב באתם עידי עיין שם גבי מה שכ' התוספת בשם ר\"ת כמו שהודה בפני עדים ואין הדמיון טוב אלא איידי דנקט לעיל דאמר אתם עידי כו' אלא ודאי ס\"ל דמה לי שמחייב עצמו בשטר בעדים לגבות ממשעבדי או שמחייב עצמו בכתב ידו לענין בני חרי כיון שכותב כן בכתב ידו: ובזה ניחא הא דכ' הטור לקמן סי' ס' ס\"ט המחייב עצמו כו' וכ\"כ הרמב\"ן ז\"ל כו' לפיכך אם לא קנו מידו ולא חייב עצמו בשטר גובה מבני חורין אבל אם קנו מידו או שחייב עצמו בשטר גובה ממשועבדים עכ\"ל שהוצרכו הב\"י והב\"ח ובעל גי' תרומה שער ס\"ד חלק א' דף שמ\"ו ע\"ד ושאר אחרונים לדחוק שאין זה מלשון הרמב\"ן אלא מלשון הטור עצמו שהרי ה' המגיד כ' פי\"א מה' מכירה שלדעת הרמב\"ן א\"א להתחייב שלא בשטר בדבר שאינו חייב בו ע\"כ דבריהם ולפי ע\"ד בחנם דחקו דלא בא ה' המגיד בשם הרמב\"ן אלא לאפוקי אתם עידי או כשאמר לשון זה אני חייב לך מנה בשטר אבל כשכ' לו כתב ידו להתחייב משמע להדיא מדברי ה' המגיד שם דאף להרמב\"ן גובה מבני חרי ע\"ש א\"כ הטור לקמן סי' ס' מיירי כשחייב עצמו בכתב ידו וכן עיקר:"]
[" שהרי חייב עצמו כמו שישתעבד הערב. נראה דכונת הרמב\"ם בזה להוכיח דסוגיא דר\"פ הנושא מיירי במחייב עצמו בדבר שלא הי' חייב מדפריך התם מערב וכמ\"ש בהרי\"ף ראיה זו ע\"ש:"]
[" כמו שישתעבד הערב כו'. כתב הסמ\"ע פירוש כשקודם שחתמו העדים כ' בשטר פלוני לוה מפ' ופ' ערב ואח\"כ חתמו העדים דמשתעבד הערב אף כשלא קנו מידו כיון דכתב ליה בשטר כו' ולא דק דהא ס\"ל להרמב\"ם והטור והמחבר לקמן סי' קכ\"ט ס\"ד דצריך קנין בערב היוצא קודם חיתום שטרות אלא כוונת הרמב\"ם והט\"ו כאן לומר שהרי חייב עצמו אע\"פ שאינו חייב כמו שישתעבד הערב אע\"פ שאינו חייב וק\"ל:"]
siftei_kohen.en:
One who obligates himself, etc. This means that he knows he does not presently owe the other person anything and voluntarily creates a new obligation, like a gift. But if one admits to his fellow under the assumption that he already owes him, and afterward it becomes known that he was mistaken, whether the mistake is established by witnesses or the supposed creditor admits that nothing was owed, this is an admission made in error and is entirely ineffective. This is so even if he delivered a document before witnesses and witnesses signed it, as the Tur writes. The rule is straightforward from below, siman 126, seif 3, and many other places: every kinyan made in error is reversed.
How? One who says to witnesses, etc. The Sema writes that many authorities disagree with this and hold that a person who seeks to create a new obligation can do so only if he writes it in a document, or if he says, "I owe you one hundred by document," etc. The Sema was not precise. He should have written that those authorities hold that even saying, "I owe you one hundred by document," is ineffective, and that only an actual written document works. Maggid Mishneh, chapter 11 of Hilchot Mechirah, explicitly says so in the name of Ramban, Rashba, and other commentators. He concludes that according to this approach there is no way for the person to become obligated except by actually writing a document. They therefore disagree with the Mechaber in two of his three categories. Ran at the beginning of chapter HaNose likewise writes according to this approach that words alone cannot create a new monetary obligation; there must be receipt of money, a kinyan, or a document. According to Rashi, no form of present self obligation without a kinyan is effective, as Beit Yosef explains Rashi. Shiltei Giborim at the beginning of chapter HaNose similarly rules in the name of Riaz that one who seeks to obligate himself in something he does not already owe, saying, "I hereby obligate myself to give you one hundred," does not become liable merely by saying "You are my witnesses," and even a signed document delivered to the recipient does not create the obligation unless a kinyan is made, according to Beit Hillel. See Ritva at the beginning of chapter HaNose and see below, seif katan 5.
One who says to witnesses, "Be witnesses for me that I owe so and so one hundred," etc. In this first category, and in the third category where he says before witnesses, "I hereby owe you one hundred by document," the creditor may collect only from unencumbered property. In the middle category, where the obligor writes in a document, "I owe you one hundred," and delivers that document in the presence of witnesses, the creditor may collect from encumbered property according to the view that witnesses to delivery give the document its legal force, even if the writing is not in the obligor's own hand. If he did not deliver it before witnesses, the creditor may collect from unencumbered property if it is in the obligor's handwriting, as I explain below, seif katan 5. Ramban and Rashba agree to this middle category. So too do Ran and Maggid Mishneh, as well as Tosafot in the name of Rabbeinu Tam, the Rosh, the Tur, and the other authorities. Ritva at the beginning of chapter HaNose writes that Rabbeinu Tam's approach is correct. This is the primary law, contrary to Shiltei Giborim cited in the preceding seif katan. The same is true if witnesses themselves wrote a document stating that the obligor created a new obligation and instructed them to write it. This is effective even according to Ramban, Rashba, and the authorities who follow them. Ran at the beginning of chapter HaNose clearly implies this. See there carefully.
"Be witnesses for me," etc. Maggid Mishneh writes that Ramban, Rashba, and other commentators disagree and bring proofs that a person cannot create a new obligation through words alone, even by saying "You are my witnesses," without a kinyan or written document. Perhaps their proofs are those brought by Ran at the beginning of chapter HaNose. A guarantor, for example, generally requires either a kinyan or the benefit he receives when money is advanced in reliance upon him. Likewise, the Gemara in chapter HaZahav, concerning custodians of land, establishes the case as one where a kinyan was made from them. In chapter HaShoel, when a gratuitous custodian stipulates to have the liability of a borrower, the Gemara asks, "By what means? By mere words?" and answers that the custodian accepts liability in exchange for the benefit of being trusted. Ran ultimately explains that according to Rif and Rambam, when the Gemara establishes the land custodian's undertaking through a kinyan, it need not mean that a kinyan is the only possible mechanism. Saying "You are my witnesses" could likewise work, for on the same logic the Gemara could have established it where he obligated himself by document, since we rule like Rabbi Yochanan. The Gemara chose a kinyan because that is the most common form of acquisition. A guarantor differs because his obligation resembles an asmachta, and therefore "You are my witnesses" alone is insufficient. In my view, Rif and Rambam can be explained more sharply. Only here, where a person creates an immediate and unconditional obligation, can a written self obligation or "You are my witnesses" be effective. A land custodian or borrower does not become liable immediately, but only if a future loss occurs, which resembles the conditional undertaking of a guarantor and therefore has an asmachta character. A kinyan is required there. Rambam's own wording is precise. He begins: "One who obligates himself in money to another without any condition at all is liable, for this is a gift and not an asmachta. How? One who says to witnesses, etc." Why stress "without any condition" and "not an asmachta" unless he intends this very distinction? Rabbeinu Yerucham, netiv 15, part 3, also cites this language. This appears clear.
Or he wrote it for him in a document, etc. The Bach writes that this works only where the document is in the obligor's own handwriting. If it is not in his handwriting and he did not personally sign beneath it, the Tur implies that according to Rabbeinu Tam, even if he delivered it before witnesses he cannot collect even from unencumbered property, because the obligor can say, "I was merely jesting with you." The Bach says Mordechai states this explicitly and Hagahot Ashri likewise. I am astonished by this. According to the view that witnesses to delivery create the legal force of a document, why should the absence of the obligor's handwriting matter? Once he delivered it before witnesses, the delivery witnesses create public notice and the creditor can collect even from encumbered property. A plea of jesting has no place in such a case. Even according to the Sema's version of the Mechaber below, seif 2, requiring the writing to be such that it cannot be forged, that condition addresses the possibility of alteration, as the Sema explains there, seif katan 6. Apart from forgery, collection can be made even from encumbered property although it is not the borrower's handwriting. The Tur explicitly states at the end of siman 69 that even when a document is not in the borrower's handwriting, witnesses to delivery give it force. The same must be true here. There is no reasonable basis to distinguish for this purpose between one who already owes and one who is creating an obligation now. Beit Yosef likewise writes at the end of this siman that Rambam would agree with Rabbeinu Tam's rule that if one writes in his own hand, "I, so and so, owe you one hundred," and delivers the document before witnesses, it is treated as a documented loan. The fact that it is in his handwriting certainly does not diminish it. Although its language is not ordinary document language, its written admission combined with delivery before witnesses suffices. Beit Yosef clearly understands that the essential force for encumbered property comes from the delivery witnesses. The Bach may have inferred his position from Mordechai and Hagahot Ashri asking, according to Rashi, that if the person did not sign beneath the writing he should be able to say, "I was jesting with you." One might ask why that defense exists if the writing was delivered before witnesses. But the inference is not compelling. They may understand the sugya according to the authority who does not hold that delivery witnesses create a document. If delivery witnesses did create the document, Reish Lakish's exemption would be difficult on any explanation. Rabbeinu Tam's explanation avoids that difficulty because the case concerns a newly created obligation. Moreover, below in siman 81, seif 19, seif katan 49, I have already refuted the words of Mordechai and Hagahot Ashri from Rashi, Tosafot, and other authorities. The Bach's statement that Mordechai and Hagahot Ashri explicitly support him is also inaccurate. They do not mention delivery witnesses at all. They cite Rabbeinu Tam that one creates the obligation by writing in his own hand, "I, so and so, owe you one hundred," and signing beneath it, which concerns collection from unencumbered property, as the Tur writes in Rabbeinu Tam's name. Tosafot and the Rosh at the beginning of chapter HaNose can likewise be explained this way. This also resolves Tosafot's difficulty there, 102a. Tosafot asks that if Rabbeinu Tam treats the written guaranty as a complete document creating the obligation when delivered before witnesses, then the same logic should create a lien upon encumbered property, because delivery witnesses generate public notice just as in an ordinary loan. According to what I have explained there is no difficulty. The guaranty case need not involve delivery before witnesses; it may simply be a handwritten statement, "I am guarantor." I later saw that Chochmat Shlomo and the novellae of Maharsha noticed this point. The Tur writes: "Rabbeinu Tam explains that the passage does not discuss an admission of an existing debt, but a person who now obligates himself for one hundred and writes in his own hand, 'I, so and so, owe you,' and delivers the document. By delivery of this document he now becomes liable for one hundred. If he delivers it before witnesses, collection may be made from encumbered property. If he delivers it privately, collection is from unencumbered property." The Bach understood the requirement of the obligor's handwriting as applying even where there are delivery witnesses. That is not the Tur's intent. The Tur had just cited Rashi's explanation, which requires a case not in the obligor's own handwriting, because if it were in his handwriting he would already be liable by his admission even without delivery witnesses, and Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan could not meaningfully dispute it, since the Mishnah states that one who produces a person's handwriting collects from unencumbered property. The Tur therefore says that Rabbeinu Tam avoids that forced limitation. Even if it is the obligor's handwriting, the authorities can still dispute because he is not admitting an old debt, but creating a new one through this writing. When the document is delivered before witnesses, the dispute can concern collection from encumbered property; when delivered privately, it concerns unencumbered property. The Tur had to mention handwriting for the private delivery case. But if it is delivered before witnesses, there is no need that the writing be his own. Any text incapable of alteration can create a lien according to the view that delivery witnesses give documents force. A clear proof is Maggid Mishneh, chapter 11 of Hilchot Mechirah. He writes that if the obligor writes, "I hereby owe you one hundred," even if there are no witnesses signed in the document, the recipient acquires the right. This is what Rambam means by "or he wrote him a document." Maggid Mishneh adds that this works only if he delivers the document before witnesses, according to the view that delivery witnesses effect acquisition, or alternatively if the document is in the obligor's own handwriting and he gives it privately, in which case it allows collection from unencumbered property. If another person wrote it and it was delivered privately, it is certainly ineffective. Beit Yosef and Darkei Moshe cite this. Although Maggid Mishneh writes it according to Rambam and elsewhere says Ramban and Rashba dispute Rambam, they plainly dispute only Rambam's first and third categories, namely words alone with "You are my witnesses" or an oral statement "I owe you one hundred by document." Maggid Mishneh explicitly says they agree to the middle category of an actual document. Rabbeinu Tam therefore certainly agrees as well. It also follows that one who writes the obligation in his own hand and delivers it privately creates an obligation collectible from unencumbered property even according to Ramban and Rashba. Maggid Mishneh's wording proves this, and the Tur's presentation of Rabbeinu Tam proves the same. Rabbeinu Tam himself agrees with Ramban and Rashba in Tosafot, chapter HaNose, that a new obligation cannot be created merely by saying "You are my witnesses." The difference between creating a debt through a formal document before witnesses and creating it through one's own handwriting for unencumbered property is therefore not substantive. This also resolves the Tur's language below, siman 60, seif 9, concerning one who obligates himself, where the Tur cites Ramban and then says that if no kinyan was made and he did not obligate himself "by document," collection is from unencumbered property, whereas if a kinyan was made or he obligated himself by document, collection is from encumbered property. Beit Yosef, the Bach, Gidulei Terumah, gate 64, part 1, page 346, and other later authorities were forced to say that this latter sentence is the Tur's own language and not Ramban's, because Maggid Mishneh says that Ramban does not allow a new obligation without a document. In my humble opinion their difficulty is unnecessary. Maggid Mishneh excludes only oral "You are my witnesses" and an oral statement, "I owe you one hundred by document." A handwritten self obligation, however, allows collection from unencumbered property even according to Ramban, as Maggid Mishneh himself implies. The Tur in siman 60 therefore speaks of such handwriting. This is the primary rule.
For he obligated himself just as a guarantor becomes obligated. Rambam's intent appears to be to prove that the sugya at the beginning of chapter HaNose discusses a person creating an obligation he did not previously owe, because the Gemara there challenges the rule from the law of a guarantor. Rif uses this proof as well. See there.
Just as a guarantor becomes obligated, etc. The Sema explains this as referring to a case where, before the witnesses signed, the document stated, "So and so borrowed from so and so, and so and so is guarantor," after which the witnesses signed. He says the guarantor becomes bound even without a kinyan because his obligation appears in the document. This is inaccurate. Rambam, the Tur, and the Mechaber below, siman 129, seif 4, hold that a guarantor whose undertaking appears before the witnesses' signatures still requires a kinyan in the relevant case. Rambam and the Tur and Mechaber here mean only a conceptual comparison: a person can obligate himself even though he was not previously liable, just as a guarantor assumes liability even though the principal debt was never his. This is straightforward.

turei_zahav.he: בב"י ד"ה האומר לחבירו חייב אני לך וכו' עד ואינו כתב ידו כלומר וכו') יש לפרש הל' כפשוטו דהא לקמן סימן ס"ט ס"ה פסק בשם הרמב"ן דכתיבת ידו מהני אפילו בלא חתם והעתיק ב"י בסעיף א' שם ל' בעה"ת בשם הרמב"ן שכן פרש"י ג"כ ע"ש א"כ כוונתו כאן אעפ"י שאינו כ"י דאלו הוי כ"י הוי כחתם ומה שפרש"י בהנושא דאלו חתם בו כו' ר"ל כ"י דהוה כחתם ודוק:
turei_zahav.en: In the Beit Yosef. In the passage beginning, "One who says to his fellow, I owe you," etc., until "and it is not his handwriting, meaning," etc. The wording can be understood literally. Below, siman 69, seif 5, the Shulchan Aruch rules in the name of Ramban that one's handwriting is effective even without a signature. The Beit Yosef there, in seif 1, cites Baal HaTerumot in the name of Ramban that Rashi explained likewise. Accordingly, Rambam's intention here is that even though it is not his handwriting, it is effective. If it were his handwriting, it would be like a signature. When Rashi explains in Perek HaNose that had he signed it, etc., his meaning is handwriting, which is equivalent to a signature. Examine carefully.

urim_vetumim_tumim.he:

אני מכל מקום בלשון שעבוד מהני ובן ננס פליג בתרתי ולכך פליג באחר חיתום דשייך בי' שני מחלוקת וכמ"ש התו' לפיר"ת ולמה בחרו התו' לומר ברש"י תי' אחר ונראה דקו' התו' דשם סוף ב"ב אמרינן דר"י אמר שמואל סבירא ממשעבדי ולכך תי' התו' דקודם חיתום אין רגיל ליכתוב לשון גרוע ומהני ע"מ וגובה ממשעבדי ולפ"ז דר"י סבירא ליה ע"מ כרתי יפה הקשה לר"ת דלר"א עדים שחתמו שטר לא משוי שיעבוד כלל אם אין ע"מ והוי כחספא בעלמא רק בשטר ראיה מהני דלא איברי סהדי אלא לשקר' ואם כן ר"ת דפליגי בשעבוד דמשעבד עצמו לאחר חיתום שטרות שיהיה ערב ובאמירה בע"פ לא משתעבד רק בשטר דאלים מילתא דשטר' להשתעבד ואם כן לר"א אפילו חתומים עליו עדים לא מהני לשויה שטר ולשעבד בו דאין ע"ח עושי' קנין כלל וגם לא שיעבוד והא זה שטר קנין ולא שטר ראי' ולכך מצריך ליה גמרא שיהיה ספר המקנה כמ"ש התו' ואם כן דאין ע"ח מועיל מכ"ש דאין כת"י מועיל דלא עדיף כת"י מע"ח וכן בגט לר"א כתב בכתב ידו ואין ע"מ אין מועיל עיין בא"ע סי' ק"ל ס"כ ובאחרוני' וע"כ צריך ע"מ לשויה ליה שעבוד ואם כן דישנו ע"מ אף ממשעבדי יגבה וקו' התו' דבממ"נ אי לא היה ע"מ אין כאן שטר כלל ולא משוי ליה שיעבוד כלל דע"ח לא משוי שטר כלל ואפילו מב"ח לא יגבה דהא לא נשתעבד כלל והוי כמילתא דע"פ ומכ"ש בכת"י בלי עדים ואי דישנו לע"מ אם כן מה בכך דכת בו בכת"י יגבה ממשעבדי בע"מ וקו' חזקה היא לר"ת דכתוב בכת"י ומסרו בעדים גובה לר"א ממשעבדי ועי"ל בסי' קכ"ע מ"ש לישב קו' זו ותמהני מן חכמים הנ"ל שהעלימו עין מדברים אלו ומהרש"ל שלח ידו להגיה בתו' דקו' הוא לפירש"י וזה אינו כמ"ש דלרש"י לשון גרוע לא מהני ע"מ ומ"מ אף להב"ח יש מקום לדבריו במרדכי ול"ק קו' הש"ך דהוי ע"מ כמ"ש אך מכל מקום לדינא מסתימ' כל הפוסקים לא משמע כן דבעי יחוד לע"מ אף דכתבתי לעיל כן בשם הרשב"א אולי יש לחלק ובקושי' התו' על ר"ת הנ"ל עמש"ל בסי' נ"א וסי' קכ"ט אי בעינן דוקא ע"מ לר"א ועמש"ל בסי' פ"א בתומים ס"ק כ"ה דבמעשה לא חיישינן להשטאה ולק"מ ע"ש ולכך אין מקום לדברי הב"ח:

Even though he had not owed him anything, etc. The Shach writes in seif katan 1 that if a person admitted in error, believing that he owed money when in fact he did not, and this was established by witnesses, or the creditor admitted that nothing was owed, the person is exempt. This is correct, but the Shach should have explained that when the creditor admits that nothing was owed, he must also admit that the original admission was made in error. If the creditor admits only that there had previously been no debt, that proves nothing, because a person can obligate himself even where he previously owed nothing. Thus, when the Tur says that the matter was established by witnesses or the creditor admitted that he did not owe him, the meaning is that it was also established or admitted that the original admission was mistaken. Otherwise the debtor cannot simply claim, "I was mistaken," unless he has a migo, and even there the authorities dispute the matter below in siman 81. The Sema in the Derishah wished to explain the Tur's statement, "or the creditor admitted," according to Rashi, while according to Rabbeinu Tam the creditor's admission would not suffice and witnesses would be required. He therefore explains why Baal HaTerumot, who follows Rabbeinu Tam, mentions only proof by witnesses. This seems to assume that the creditor admitted merely that no prior debt existed, but did not admit that the debtor had been mistaken, and that according to Rashi a person cannot newly obligate himself without a kinyan when nothing was previously owed. This interpretation does not work. If the witnesses testify that they know he was mistaken and that the admission was made in error, this is equivalent to the creditor himself admitting that the admission was mistaken. If, however, the witnesses merely know that no prior debt existed, that does not help according to Rabbeinu Tam, as explained. Moreover, it is clear that even according to Rashi, if a person formally admits that he owes one hundred to another, although in truth he previously owed nothing, he nevertheless becomes obligated so long as the admission was not mistaken. Otherwise Rabbeinu Tam could not have brought a proof for his own explanation from the Yerushalmi, which states that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish agree that one who admitted owing one hundred because he assumed he owed it, and it was then found that he did not, is exempt. Were Rashi's view that a new obligation cannot arise through admission, that Yerushalmi would instead be decisive support for Rashi, because the Bavli could then be reconciled simply: in the Bavli Rabbi Yochanan obligates only where the creditor asserts that there really is a debt, while the Yerushalmi exempts when it is established that no debt ever existed. Rabbeinu Tam could not cite it as a proof against Rashi. It is therefore clear that Rashi agrees that a proper admission can create liability even if no prior debt existed. The Yerushalmi's exemption concerns a demonstrated mistaken admission. This must also be so from the Gemara's challenge from the case of one who writes to a kohen that he owes five selaim. Why should that difficulty be resolved according to Rabbi Yochanan if the kohen admits that no debt exists apart from pidyon haben? If the son is not thereby redeemed, why should the father be obligated? The question applies to all views unless a formal admission can itself create liability. The same is implied by the admission used by Issur Ger in Bava Batra 149. That device appears to work without a kinyan. If there had been a kinyan, its effectiveness would be obvious, especially since a partial deathbed gift made with a kinyan is irrevocable even if the giver recovers. The entire proof from Rav Mari would be unnecessary. It follows that the formula of admission itself is not a kinyan, yet it creates liability. All the poskim cite the incident of Issur as proof of this. The question is different where one does not speak in the form of an admission but says expressly, "I hereby obligate myself to give you such and such," creating a new obligation. Riaz, cited by Shiltei Gibborim and by the Shach in seif katan 2, writes that if one says, "I am obligated to give you one hundred," when he actually owes nothing, even if he delivers a signed document, nothing takes effect without a kinyan. Tosafos also appears to imply this according to the Derishah's reading of Rabbeinu Tam. One might therefore think that this is Rashi's conclusion as well. That conclusion, however, is difficult. Rashi explains in Ketubot that a shtar haknaah may be written whether the borrower ultimately borrows or not, which indicates that the obligation can arise through the document itself. Even if one forces that case into a kinyan, there remains Abaye's principle that the witnesses' signatures create rights from the time of signing. If according to Rashi delivery of a document saying, "I owe you one hundred," cannot obligate a person where no money was lent, how could any lien arise before funds were advanced? Similarly, in the case of a document written in trust, Rashi explains that the lien can arise immediately even though the loan will take place later. This points strongly to the ability of a document to create a new obligation. One could answer that Rashi speaks only of an instrument accompanied by a kinyan, and that Abaye's rule is a special enactment whose underlying reason is not extended elsewhere. But this is strained. The language of Tosafos also indicates that the Yerushalmi is a support for Rabbeinu Tam only if Rashi agrees that a formal written obligation can create liability. Otherwise the Yerushalmi would support Rashi rather than Rabbeinu Tam. It therefore appears clear that where the obligation is created in a full document executed by witnesses, the person may obligate himself even though no previous debt existed. The question concerns a mere handwritten instrument. Rashi need not hold that a simple handwritten note, without witnesses, is sufficiently powerful to create a new obligation. Tosafos at the end of Perek Get Pashut states that a loan without witnesses does not create a Torah level lien, indicating that a handwritten note lacks the full force of a witnessed document. Accordingly, there is a genuine distinction between Rashi and Rabbeinu Tam. According to Rabbeinu Tam, their dispute concerns one who writes in his own hand a new obligation even though he previously owed nothing, because the Gemara compares the case to a guarantor after the signatures, which is essentially a written self obligation. According to Rashi, by contrast, their dispute concerns an admission, and from Rashi's explanation there is no basis to say that a mere handwritten document can itself create a new obligation. A full document executed by witnesses can do so. This also fits the language of the Rosh, who, when explaining Rabbeinu Tam, says expressly that the person wrote in his own hand. His question, "How can he obligate movable property through this document?" refers specifically to this inferior handwritten instrument, not to a full witnessed document. A full document creates a lien on land, and land can be acquired through a document. This appears to me the correct distinction.
Thus, where the language is one of admission, even a handwritten instrument can obligate according to Rashi, because admission itself has the force of one hundred witnesses. The case of the five selaim owed to the kohen is according to Rashi a handwritten instrument, yet Rabbi Yochanan obligates even though there was no prior debt. By contrast, a newly created obligation in the form, "I obligate myself," requires a full document with witnesses according to Rashi, while Rabbeinu Tam allows even the handwritten instrument. Be witnesses for me, etc. If one merely says, "Be witnesses for me," or "I hereby owe you one hundred by document," this does not by itself create a lien on real property, as the Shach writes. At first sight this is difficult from the Gemara's proof from one who marries a woman and undertakes to support her daughter. The Gemara initially assumes a case of this kind, according to Rambam, meaning that he says, "I owe you by document." Why then can the daughter collect from encumbered property? If the commitment was written explicitly in a proper document there would be no proof. One answer is that the initial assumption was that, like a sale made before witnesses, such a public undertaking has a voice and therefore can be collected from encumbered property. Tosafos in Gittin 51 uses this reasoning. A more satisfactory explanation is that the baraita's statement that after the parties die she is supported from encumbered property means only that there exists a legal possibility of such collection, namely where a kinyan was made. With a stepdaughter, a kinyan can create collection from encumbered property; with one's own daughters, there is no equivalent arrangement. Thus the statement does not mean that an ordinary oral undertaking always collects from encumbered property. Tosafos in Ketubot 102 explicitly explains that without a written instrument one collects only from unencumbered property, and that the case there happened to involve a kinyan. Rambam's commentary on the Mishnah likewise supports this understanding.
Or he wrote to him, etc. Mordechai, cited in Hagahot Ashri, asks according to Rashi, who explains the case as one where the person did not sign: through what act does he become obligated? Why can he not say, "I was merely joking with you"? Mordechai therefore adopts Rabbeinu Tam's explanation that the entire discussion concerns a person who admits that he previously owed nothing and now wishes to create a new obligation, and "one hundred by document" means that he executed a full document of obligation despite the absence of a prior debt. The Bach inferred from Mordechai that according to Rabbeinu Tam, if the person did not sign the instrument, even delivery before witnesses is ineffective. The Shach objects that since we rule that witnesses to delivery effect the document, a writing delivered before witnesses is a full document even if it is not signed and even if it is not in the obligor's handwriting, provided it cannot be forged. The Shach therefore says that Mordechai's challenge to Rashi must have been according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that witnesses to signature effect the instrument. That answer is difficult. It would make the entire dispute of Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish depend upon Rabbi Meir, while according to Rabbi Elazar Reish Lakish would concede. The Gemara could then answer every challenge simply by saying that the source follows Rabbi Elazar. Moreover, the entire dispute would be contrary to our ruling like Rabbi Elazar. Tosafos already addressed this in Ketubot. They explain that the phrase used in the document is an inferior or incomplete expression, one that does not constitute a proper dispositive document merely because it was delivered before witnesses. That is why Reish Lakish can say that it creates no obligation, while Rabbi Yochanan nevertheless gives it force. This also explains why the Gemara compares the matter to a guarantor who writes his guarantee after the signatures. It is not the ordinary dispute between signature witnesses and delivery witnesses. There are two ways to understand Tosafos's further question against Rabbeinu Tam from the guarantor case. First, as explained above in simanim 43 and 45, even a handwritten document can create a danger of an earlier date being used for a later obligation. A loan document without a kinyan may not be delivered to the borrower for later use, because he might write in Nisan and borrow only in Tishrei, thereby improperly collecting from purchasers. Where a guarantor appears in the document without a kinyan, the same concern applies to the guarantor's property. The witnesses must therefore deliver the document to the lender on the day of the loan. That delivery itself is the clearest form of witnesses to delivery. If so, even wording such as "So and so is guarantor" should create a lien through delivery witnesses. This yields Tosafos's difficulty. This remains true even if the guarantor was not physically present at the final delivery. Delivery witnesses may act through agency; a get is delivered to a wife before witnesses even when the husband is overseas. If the guarantor wrote his undertaking and gave it to the witnesses, and they then delivered the loan document to the lender, they act as his agents and as witnesses to delivery. Nor can the case be explained as a shtar haknaah or through Abaye's rule that signatures create rights from the time of signing. According to Ben Nanas, who follows Reish Lakish's premise that a person cannot create this obligation through the inferior writing itself, those devices cannot help. The obligation can arise only through delivery connected to the actual advance of money. This also explains Tosafos's statement in Ketubot that the Gemara's question, "we require a dispositive document," is directed specifically against Ben Nanas. Second, the question can be framed according to Rabbi Elazar's general rule that delivery witnesses are essential. Where the writing is not itself a full dispositive document, signature witnesses alone cannot create a new obligation, because this is not merely an evidentiary document but an instrument whose purpose is to create the obligation. If there are no delivery witnesses, it is like a shard and cannot obligate even the debtor's unencumbered property. If there are delivery witnesses, however, then according to Rabbi Elazar it should be a full document and should collect from encumbered property. This creates a dilemma for Rabbeinu Tam: without delivery witnesses, there is no effective instrument at all; with delivery witnesses, why should it collect only from unencumbered property? Mordechai may understand, however, that delivery witnesses must be specifically designated as such. Rashba, at the end of Gittin, explains that where a person writes, "I owe you one hundred that I borrowed from you in this document," he becomes obligated when he appoints witnesses and delivers it before them for the purpose that they serve as witnesses to the loan. By contrast, if witnesses merely happen to be present when the paper is handed over and were not designated for that purpose, they are not witnesses to delivery in the relevant sense. Many authorities who require a formula such as "sign and testify" likewise indicate that designation is needed. According to this approach, the guarantor case may involve witnesses who happened to be present but were not appointed as delivery witnesses, and Mordechai can therefore ask why the guarantor cannot claim that he was joking. Tosafos, however, do not appear to accept such a requirement of designation, as is evident from their question that the guarantor's document should have full force through delivery witnesses. Maharshal and Maharsha struggled with this question, while the Shach rejected Tosafos's concern by saying that the case did not involve delivery witnesses. In my view the Tosafos question can be explained in the two ways just stated and remains powerful. This also explains Tosafos's earlier question on Rashi. They ask that if the problem is merely inferior wording, the same problem should exist even when the guarantor's language appears before the signatures. One cannot answer simply that before the signatures the guarantee was made at the time the money was advanced and therefore the guarantor became obligated orally. That may create personal liability, but according to Rabbi Elazar signature witnesses alone do not create the document's lien. If the language is too defective to function through delivery witnesses, there is no proper document for collection from encumbered property. Tosafos therefore answer that before the signatures people do not ordinarily use the inferior wording, while after the signatures they may do so because the loan has already been completed. The conclusion is that the Bach's inference from Mordechai has some basis if one requires designated delivery witnesses, but as a matter of practical law the simple implication of the poskim does not support such a limitation. I have written above the Rashba's formulation, and perhaps distinctions remain. See also what I write in simanim 51 and 129 concerning whether Rabbi Elazar always requires delivery witnesses, and in siman 81 in Tumim, seif katan 25, where I explain that where there is an overt act we do not ordinarily suspect joking. Accordingly, there is no firm basis for the Bach's ruling.

המחייב וכו' דוקא בדלא טעה אבל אי טעה דחשב דהוא חייב ובאמת אינו חייב לכ"ע אין הודאתו כלום והן שנתברר ע"י עדים או שהודה המלוה דהי' בטעות ובזו ליכא מחלוקת כלל ואם אין המלוה מודה רק הוא אומר טעיתי ויש לו מגו דפרעתי ע"ל סי' פ"א ועיי' תומים מש"כ בזה בדעת רש"י ותוס':
הוי עלי עדים וכו' גובה רק במנ"ח דכל כמה דלא כתב שטר ולא מסרו לו שטר בע"מ לכ"ע גובה רק מבנ"ח ועייו תומים מ"ש בישוב דברי הרמב"ם:
שאני חייב כו' דעת רבים מפוסקים תוס' ורא"ש ורמב"ן ורשב"א חולקים בזה וס"ל כיון דאינו חייב והמלוה מודה דאינו חייב א"י להתחייב הן שאמר לו אתם עדים או שאמר לו חייב אני לך מנה בשטר מ"מ לא מתחייב עד שימסור לו שטר הן שטר בעדים חתומים או שטר בע"מ או בכת"י וחתום עליו ודלא כסמ"ע דס"ל באמר מנה בשטר אני חייב לך משתעבד לכ"ע וזהו אינו דלדעת הפוסקים הנ"ל גם זו לא מועיל עד שימסור שטר כמ"ש וכמ"ש הש"ך והסמ"ע כ' דהטור השמיט הך דינא באומר א"ע שאני חייב והוא אינו חייב משום דלס"ל כרמב"ם בזה ולא דק דבסי' סמ"ך הביאו הטור ולכן האמת דלרמב"ם בכל גווני חייב ולשיטת החולקים אינו מתחייב רק בשטר ולא זולתו וכבר תמה הסמ"ע על המחבר ורמ"א שלא זכר דעת החולקים הנ"ל והמה גדולים וכו' ופשיטא דיכול המוחזק לומר קי' לי' כוותי' וז"ל הואיל ומ"מ והר"ן כ' שדעת הרמב"ם בלישנא דגמ' סובל יותר ולכך הכריע כוותי':
או שאמר לו חייב וכו' העלה הש"ך דהא דסגי' לרמב"ם באמירה וא"צ שטר היינו כשהוא מתחייב בהחלט בלי תלי' תנאי דגמר ומשעבד אבל במתנה ש"ח להתחייב כש"ש שהוא בתלי' אם יגנב וכדומה ישלם דהוא כעין אסמכת' דחשב דלא יקרה אסון כלל בזה לא משעבד בפיו אלא בקנין או שטר אף לרמב"ם ובזה מיושב מה שטען עליו מהך מתנה ש"ח וכו':
הואיל ואמר בשטר וש"מ דאמר מנה חייב אני לך ולא אמר א"ע ולא הזכיר שטר דעת המבי"ט ח"א סימן שכ"ב הואיל ודברי ש"מ ככתובין דמי מתחייב ע"ש ודבריו צ"ע כי לפמש"ל סי' רנ"ה משמע דאף בש"מ כל זמן שלא אמר תנו או דמסר כת"י יכול לומר שלא להשביע א"ע וטענינן לבניו ולכן דבריו צל"ע:
כמו שישתעבד הערב פי' כמו דלא קיבל הערב מעות ומ"מ מתחייב אף זה אף דלא נתחייב מ"מ הרי יכול להתחייב א"ע והא דבעי בערב גופי' קנין ומה שקשה בזה מסוגית הגמרא עמש"ל סי' קכ"ט בישוב דברי הרמב"ם באריכות:
urim_vetumim_urim.en:
One who obligates himself, etc. This applies only where he was not mistaken. If he mistakenly thought he was already obligated when in truth he was not, all agree that his admission has no effect. This may be established either by witnesses or by the creditor's own admission that the statement was mistaken, and there is no dispute about this. If the creditor does not admit the mistake and only the debtor says, "I was mistaken," while having a migo that he could say, "I paid," see below in siman 81 and Tumim concerning the views of Rashi and Tosafos.
Let witnesses be upon me, etc. One may collect only from unencumbered property, because so long as he did not write and deliver a document, even one signed by witnesses of delivery, all agree there is no collection from encumbered property. See Tumim, where I reconcile Rambam's words.
That I owe, etc. Many authorities, including Tosafos, Rosh, Ramban, and Rashba, disagree with this ruling. They hold that where the person was not previously indebted and the creditor admits that no debt existed, he cannot create the obligation merely by saying, "You are witnesses," or even, "I owe you one hundred in a document." Rather, he becomes obligated only by actually delivering a document, whether a document signed by witnesses, a document established through witnesses of delivery, or a signed document in his own handwriting. This is unlike Sema, who holds that if he says, "I owe you one hundred in a document," all agree that he becomes obligated. That is incorrect, for according to the authorities listed above even this language is ineffective until a document is delivered, as the Shach writes. Sema writes that the Tur omitted the law of one who says, "You are witnesses that I owe," where no debt existed because the Tur does not accept Rambam's position. This is inaccurate, because the Tur cites the law in siman 60. The correct analysis is therefore that according to Rambam he is liable in every such formulation, whereas according to the dissenting authorities he becomes obligated only through a document and not otherwise. Sema himself wonders why the Mechaber and Rama did not mention these major dissenting authorities. Certainly the party in possession may say that he relies upon them. Nevertheless, Maggid Mishneh and Ran write that Rambam's reading fits the language of the Gemara better, and for that reason the ruling was decided in his favor.
Or if he said to him, "I am obligated," etc. Shach concludes that Rambam's rule, that oral commitment suffices without a document, applies only where a person undertakes an absolute obligation without attaching it to a condition, for then he definitively resolves to bind himself. But where an unpaid bailee agrees to become liable like a paid bailee, so that his obligation depends upon a future event, such as theft, it resembles an asmachta because he assumes that no mishap will occur. In such a case even Rambam requires a kinyan or a document. This resolves the difficulty raised against Rambam from the case of an unpaid bailee who undertakes the liability of a paid bailee.
Since he said, "in a document." It follows that if a shechiv mera said, "I owe you one hundred," without saying "you are witnesses" and without mentioning a document, Mabit, part 1, siman 322, holds that since the words of a shechiv mera are treated as written, he becomes obligated. See there. His ruling requires study, because according to what I wrote below in siman 255, even a shechiv mera who did not say, "Give," and did not deliver a handwritten acknowledgment may still say that his statement was made only to avoid appearing wealthy, and we make that claim for his heirs. His words therefore require further examination.
Like the guarantor becomes obligated. Meaning that just as a guarantor receives no money yet nevertheless becomes obligated, so too this person, although no prior debt existed, can voluntarily create an obligation upon himself. As for why a guarantor himself sometimes requires a kinyan, and the difficulty from the Gemara, see what I wrote below in siman 129 at length in explanation of Rambam.

mechaber.he: לוה שכתב בכ"י והעיד בו עדים ונתנו למלוה ה"ז שטר כשר וכן אם כתב שטר אף ע"פ שאין בו עדים ונתנו למלוה בפני עדים ה"ז מלוה בשטר והוא שיהי' כתב ידו שאינו יכול להזדייף ויקראו אותו העדים שנמסר בפניהם ויש מהגאונים שהורו שצריך לומר לעדים שמסרו בפניהם חתמו והעידו שנמסר בפניכם:
mechaber.en: If a borrower writes a document in his own hand, has witnesses attest it, and gives it to the lender, it is a valid document. Likewise, if he writes a document without signed witnesses and delivers it to the lender before witnesses, it creates a documented loan, provided that the handwriting cannot be forged and the witnesses to delivery read it. Some Geonim ruled that he must tell the witnesses before whom it was delivered, 'Sign and attest that it was delivered before you.'

baer_hetev.he:
והעיד. היינו שחתומין בו והעידו על כתב ידו כ"כ הסמ"ע. והש"ך פירש שהעיד עדים על גוף הענין לא לקיים החתימ':
כשר. לגבות בו ממשעבדי וכן מ"ש אח"ז ה"ז מלוה בשטר היינו לגבות ממשעבדי ובסעיף שלפני זה לא איירי אלא לענין חיוב בלבד. סמ"ע:
ונתנו. היינו כמ"ד עידי מסיר' כרתי אבל יש חולקין כמ"ש ס"ס נ"א וע"ש. ש"ך:
ידו. כתב הסמ"ע דבהרמב"ם והטור ליתא תיבת ידו ונרא' דהמחבר ה"ק והוא שיהי' כתוב בכ"י הלוה דאז אינו יכול לזייף בקל וכתבו הרמב"ם בשטר כזה שאין בו עדים שיהי' כתב שא"י להזדייף דאילו שטר שיש בו עדים מירתת טפי לזייף וע"ל ר"ס מ"ב והש"ך כתב דא"צ לדוחק זה אלא דעיקר טעמא הוא כיון שאין עדים חתומים בו יש לחוש שיזייף ויכתוב עוד אבל ביש בו עדים תו לא מצי למיכתב מידי בתר החתימ' ולכן בעינן כתב שא"י להזדייף שלא יכתוב עוד שום דבר יותר עכ"ל:
baer_hetev.en:
And testified. The Sema explains that this means witnesses were signed on the document and testified to the authenticity of his handwriting. The Shach explains instead that witnesses testified to the substance of the matter, not merely to authenticate the signature.
kosher. To collect it from my servants and from the High Court of Justice, we were to collect from my servants and in the previous section, not only for a deed matter. A:
We gave. “We were like a martyr, but we were divided as a snail and a fire. “Third:
His hand. The Sema notes that the word "his hand" does not appear in the Rambam or Tur. He explains that the Mechaber means that the document must be in the borrower's own handwriting, because then it is not easily falsified. The Rambam writes regarding such a document, which has no witnesses, that it must be written in a manner that cannot be altered. A document signed by witnesses creates a greater fear of falsification. See the beginning of siman 42. The Shach writes that no forced explanation is necessary. The primary reason is that since no witnesses are signed, there is concern that the holder may alter it and add text. When witnesses are signed, however, nothing can be added after the signatures. Therefore the writing must be resistant to alteration, so that no additional matter can be inserted.

beer_hagolah.he:
ג) ל' הרמב"ם בפי"א מה' מלוה ולוה וכת' ה"ה זה מוסכם בפ' המגרש (גיטין דף פו ע"א)
ד) כשמואל דאמר הל' כר"א אף בשאר שטרות כדעת רבותינו הצרפתים וכן מוכח עובדא דהנהו תרי גיסי וכו' סנהדרין (דף כ"ח ע"ב) וסוגיא שבסוף גט פשוט (בבא בתרא דף ק"ע ע"א) ושזה דעת בעה"ע ורובי המפרשים ה"ה
ה) מעובדא דשטרא דפרסאה גיטין דף י"א ע"א ושכ"כ הרי"ף בפ' המביא תניין וש"פ כר"א:
ו) כתב ה"ה נראה טעם סברא זו כדי שיהיה לזה קול ושזו היא סברת רב האי ורב שרירא ז"ל כתובה בעיטור:
beer_hagolah.en:
The language of the Rambam, chapter 11 of Hilkhot Malveh VeLoveh. The Maggid Mishneh writes that this is agreed upon in chapter HaMegaresh, Gittin 86a.
In accordance with Shmuel, who rules like Rabbi Elazar even regarding other documents, as held by the French sages. This is also proved by the incident of the two brothers-in-law, Sanhedrin 28b, and the discussion at the end of Get Pashut, Bava Batra 170a. The Maggid Mishneh writes that this is the view of the Baal HaIttur and most commentators.
From the incident of the Persian document, Gittin 11a. So too the Rif in chapter HaMevi Tinyana, and the other poskim rule like Rabbi Elazar.
He wrote, "This is a taste of this darkness so that it has a voice, and that it is a great sign of the island and a great deal of great sin."

beur_hagra.he:
לוה. גיטין פ"י א' כתב בכת"י כו' הא יש עליו עדים כשר לכתחלה ושם רא"א אע"פ שאין כו' מ' כ"ש אם יש עליו עדים שגובה ממשועבדים לד"ה:
